Chapter Four: Shaping the Environment—Making Change Easier by Tweaking the Path.
Let’s face it, even if you’ve got a rock-solid plan and you’re fired up to make a change, things can still fall apart if your environment’s working against you. The path you’re on—the context where your behavior happens—can quietly shape your actions, sometimes even more than your own determination.
Think about it: people naturally follow the path of least resistance. If you’ve got healthy snacks right where you can see and grab them, you’re far more likely to pick them up. Or, if your workplace introduces a new process that’s simple and gets plenty of support, chances are folks will actually use it. But when your surroundings are full of obstacles or temptations, even the most motivated person can find themselves struggling.
So, shaping the path is really about removing friction and making the right choice the easiest one. You can do this a few different ways:
First, by altering your physical environment. Maybe you rearrange your space, set up your tools, or organize resources so the new habit fits naturally into your day.
Next, you build habits and routines—embedding the change so deeply into your daily life that it starts to happen almost automatically.
And don’t underestimate the power of checklists or reminders. Sometimes a simple prompt is all it takes to keep your new behavior front and center.
Here’s a real-world example: imagine a hospital wants to cut down on infections. Instead of just telling staff to wash their hands more, they put hand sanitizer at every doorway and add visual cues as reminders. These small tweaks to the environment can lead to big shifts in how people behave.
Social influences matter just as much. We’re all more likely to change if we see others doing it first. That’s why visible examples—like celebrating teams who hit safety goals—can kick-start even wider adoption.
Sometimes, shaping the path is about changing the order of steps. If a company needs reports on time, maybe they tweak deadlines or set up automatic reminders. For a family trying to eat healthier, it could mean planning meals ahead and keeping good food stocked up.
When you focus on your environment, change stops being a test of willpower. It becomes about making the right choice feel easy—relieving the pressure on both your thoughtful “rider” and your emotional “elephant.” And that’s how you really boost your chances for lasting success.
